title: R’ Chanina Antaya or Antonya
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman cites Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 6:5. R’ Yonah and R’ Yose went up to R’ Chanina Antanya’s wedding feast. Hyman cites a lexicon under משתיתן for the gloss “to his huppah.” In the passage he cites at the end of Avodah Zarah 5:1, R’ Yose asks R’ Chanina Antonaya, “Do you remember that you and R’ Yirmeyah used to say in the name of רש״ל?” At the beginning of Terumot chapter 2 he went up with R’ Zeira [note marker ב)] to חמת דנרר, as supplied. At the end of Peah 1:1, Hyman cites “taught before R’ Mana” [note marker ב)]. He gives the reading “Rav Chananyah Mantonya taught before R’ Mana.” He also cites Shabbat 7:2, folio 28b [כח:].

notes.text: The lexicon form במעיך, place form חמת דנרר and unsupplied ב) footnotes remain unresolved. No new place identification or native reading is adopted.

No new primary scalar was returned. Hyman’s wedding-feast account concerns Chanina’s feast; the huppah gloss belongs to the unidentified lexicon. במעיך remains beside the earlier במעריך lead; neither Arukh nor Me’arekh is established. חמת דנרר is not silently changed to Hammat Gader. נהורת is contextually do you remember, without a native letter repair; רש״ל remains abbreviated. Both unsupplied ב) markers, all Antaya/Antonya/Antanya/Mantonya forms, full Rav Chananyah and28b convention remain. The earlier categorical lexicon/place repairs are rejected as unproved.

Hyman’s printed article (vol. II, p. 499) reads במעריך, whereas the supplied text has במעיך. The title points to Ma’arikh, the lexicon attributed to Menahem di Lonzano. The gloss itself is given here on Hyman’s authority. The consulted Berakhot 6:5 describes the wedding feast and the food served afterward. The consulted Avodah Zarah chapter 5 gives the question as נהירת and names Resh Lakish. Orlah chapter 2 has a parallel with a different wording of the question. In Terumot 2:1 the destination is Hammat Gader. Peah 1:1 has R’ Chananyah Antonia teaching before R’ Mana, while Hyman quotes Rav Chananyah Mantonya. Shabbat 7:2 also names Chanina Antonia. Both note markers appear in Hyman’s print, and their note text was unavailable in the supplied article.
